assertion: The Saint Paul protection arrangement originated under Police Chief John O'Connor in 1900.
supportExplanation: Minnesota Historical Society accounts document O'Connor instituting the system at the start of his tenure.
qualification: Predates national Prohibition; informal policy rather than formal municipal legislation.

assertion: Check-in, regular payments, and restraint from major crimes inside Saint Paul were the core conditions of refuge.
supportExplanation: Described in historical accounts as the three pillars of the O'Connor layover agreement.
qualification: Synthesized from historical accounts; no signed physical contract exists.

assertion: William 'Reddy' Griffin preceded Dan Hogan as the chief intermediary between criminals and police.
supportExplanation: MNHS account identifies Griffin as the initial broker until his death in 1913.
qualification: Do not collapse all earlier activity into Hogan's later saloon venue.

assertion: The Green Lantern Saloon on Wabasha Street was associated with Dan Hogan and criminal gatherings.
supportExplanation: Historical accounts document the saloon as Hogan's operational base and a prominent underworld meeting place.
qualification: No historical record claims every corrupt transaction occurred within that building.

assertion: Chief O'Connor retired in 1920; Dan Hogan was assassinated in a car bombing in 1928.
supportExplanation: Documents O'Connor's retirement and Hogan's violent death.
qualification: Hogan's bombing remains legally unsolved; no assailant was ever convicted.

assertion: The 18th Amendment was ratified in 1919 taking effect in 1920; the 21st Amendment repealed it on December 5, 1933.
locators: S13, Amendments XVIII and XXI annotations
supportExplanation: Official constitutional records of ratification and repeal dates.
qualification: Constitutional prohibition differs from the statutory Volstead Act; June 1933 preceded repeal.

assertion: Hotel history associates Leon Gleckman's headquarters and Treasury agent Malone's surveillance with the Saint Paul Hotel.
supportExplanation: Institutional retrospective records the suite association and surveillance.
qualification: Institutional account; no specific permanent suite number or staff complicity established.

assertion: Federal tax prosecution of Gleckman required distinguishing gross bank deposits from net taxable income.
supportExplanation: Appellate court held that bank deposits alone do not constitute taxable income without eliminating loans and capital.
qualification: Reflects the specific appellate holding in that proceeding.

assertion: Gleckman's federal tax convictions were affirmed for 1929 and 1930, while he was acquitted on the 1931 count.
supportExplanation: Eighth Circuit formal disposition affirmed convictions on counts 1 and 2, noting acquittal on count 3.
qualification: Preserve the partial acquittal; do not misrepresent as conviction on all counts.

assertion: Gleckman's criminal contempt convictions for jury tampering were affirmed on appeal in 1938.
supportExplanation: Appellate record details payments and credit extended to juror Fuchs following a 1934 mistrial.
qualification: Adjudicated under criminal contempt rather than a separate statutory bribery indictment.

assertion: Gleckman and first trial jurors lodged at the Saint Paul Hotel during proceedings.
supportExplanation: Contempt opinion records physical proximity of defendant and jurors at the hotel.
qualification: Proximity is not proof of hotel management complicity.

assertion: Castle Royal, Inc. corporate notice was published in Commercial West on September 30, 1933.
supportExplanation: Contemporaneous corporate incorporation notice in financial press.
qualification: Documents corporate formation; does not prove opening date or patrons.

assertion: Historian Greg Brick dates Castle Royal nightclub opening to October 26, 1933.
supportExplanation: Scholarly study of Twin Cities subterranean venues provides opening date.
qualification: Attributed to Brick's historical monograph.

assertion: Famous gangsters such as John Dillinger or Ma Barker frequented Castle Royal as patrons.
supportExplanation: Historian Greg Brick and Paul Maccabee found no documentation proving attendance; claims emerged in 1970s promotional nostalgia.
qualification: Remains disputed/unverified folklore; must not be stated as factual history.

assertion: William Hamm Jr. was kidnapped on June 15, 1933, held for $100,000 ransom, and released alive.
supportExplanation: Both local historical society and FBI records confirm abduction, ransom, and release.
qualification: Release unharmed does not negate captivity trauma.

assertion: Historical accounts associate William Hamm Jr.'s abduction point with 671 Cable Street (later Greenbrier).
supportExplanation: Ramsey County History documents the residence location as the abduction site.
qualification: Site of abduction was residential; the brewery complex is a contextual landmark.

assertion: FBI investigators visualized latent fingerprints on Hamm ransom letters using silver nitrate.
supportExplanation: FBI case history credits silver nitrate development with establishing Barker-Karpis culpability.
qualification: Institutional agency account; not an assertion of being the first in all world forensic history.

assertion: Edward Bremer was kidnapped on January 17, 1934 at Lexington and Goodrich after dropping his daughter at school.
supportExplanation: Federal investigative summary documents exact date, location, and circumstances.
qualification: Date is January 17, 1934; corrects printing error in S08.

assertion: Investigators reported Harry Sawyer advocated kidnapping Bremer over robbing Commercial State Bank for larger returns.
supportExplanation: Federal summary records Sawyer's calculation of expected extortion yield.
qualification: Attributed to post-arrest investigative reports, not a wiretap transcript.

assertion: Bremer kidnappers demanded $200,000 ransom and coerced Walter Magee under threats of violence against police contact.
supportExplanation: Federal summary documents ransom letters and coercive threats against reporting.
qualification: Threats were coercive tactics; captor promises were not factual findings.

assertion: Local and federal authorities were notified immediately by Walter Magee and the Bremer family upon receipt of threats.
supportExplanation: Investigation summary confirms law enforcement was engaged despite extortionists' warnings.
qualification: Captor demands for secrecy did not produce compliance.

assertion: Edward Bremer was released by his captors after approximately three weeks of captivity following ransom payment.
supportExplanation: Agency case overview confirms duration of captivity and release in Wisconsin.
qualification: Rounded duration; exact daily release log not essential to tour.

assertion: Interstate transportation of a stolen car under the Dyer Act provided federal jurisdiction to hunt Dillinger.
locators: S11, 'The Bureau Actively Joins the Hunt'
supportExplanation: FBI history details how crossing state lines with the Lake County sheriff's vehicle triggered federal authority.
qualification: Does not imply municipal officers were legally prohibited from assisting.

assertion: Manager report on March 30, 1934 led to the March 31 shootout and Dillinger's escape at Lincoln Court.
locators: S11, Dillinger narrative; S16 address lead
supportExplanation: Documented sequence of tenant report, agent stakeout, and doorway gunfire at 93 S Lexington.
qualification: Building interior floor plan unverified; sequence drawn from agency accounts.

assertion: Evelyn Frechette was convicted of conspiracy to harbor a federal fugitive, sentenced to two years and fined $1,000.
supportExplanation: Federal record documents harboring conviction and sentence in May 1934.
qualification: Specific legal charge was harboring a fugitive, not participating in bank heists.

assertion: Saint Paul's former federal courthouse (now Landmark Center) served as the venue for Frechette's trial.
locators: S14, closing caption and historical notes
supportExplanation: Library of Congress history identifies Landmark Center as the trial location.
qualification: Building association established; specific courtroom chamber unverified.

assertion: Federal wiretap investigations in 1935 exposed Saint Paul police corruption, leading to disciplinary actions.
supportExplanation: MNHS account describes clandestine telephone taps revealing officer complicity with underworld figures.
qualification: Specific names and transcripts subject to archival qualification.

assertion: Saint Paul voters approved a charter amendment on June 15, 1936 instituting civil service rules for police chief selection and tenure.
supportExplanation: MNHS history details the transition from political appointment to competitive examination and 6-year terms.
qualification: Structural administrative reform; did not instantly eradicate all vice.

assertion: Ma Barker functioned as the criminal mastermind and tactical leader of the Barker-Karpis gang.
supportExplanation: Historians and surviving gang accounts indicate Karpis and Fred Barker directed operations; Ma Barker's mastermind role was largely an FBI media narrative.
qualification: Disputed folklore; do not present as an established historical fact.

assertion: Minnesota Historical Society interprets the Hamm and Bremer kidnappings as the breakdown of the O'Connor layover arrangement.
supportExplanation: Historical analysis views violent local kidnappings as shattering the covenant of immunity within the city.
qualification: Historical interpretation; reflects the erosion of boundaries rather than a single sudden decree.
